catalog_quote: 2.3. Prosody. There are 4 contrastive tones in Kaliko viz. Low, Mid, High and Rising (the latter being fairly marginal), as shown in the following examples: contrast Low/Mid: lāzà (to cut) làzà (to read); ndrōzà (to suck) ndròzà (to gossip). contrast High/Low: ɓá (person) ɓà (house, village); élé (dry season) èlè ('you (pl.) have left'). contrast High/Rising: àɓó (pride) àɓǒ (pigeon). contrast Low/Mid/Rising: mbà ('he has gone up') mbā ('it has grown') mbǎ (moon). 2.4 Syllable Structure. The canonical shape of Kaliko syllables is CV ... Other occurring structures are V, CGV and GV. [p. 48] ... It should be observed that (i) and (ii) above are responsible for the creation of the phonemic contour tone in Kaliko (Rising Tone; LH) as well as the emergence of a rather marginal Falling Tone (HL). That is, vowels may be deleted or devocalized but the tones associated with them do not disappear. Instead, they are attached to the tones of the neighbouring vowels. [p. 49]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kaliko (Omi) is described as a register tone language with three level tones (Low, Mid, High) plus a marginal rising contour created by vowel deletion; the description's only prosody section is about tone and it contains no statement about word stress or accent at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress rule is stated). Tone diacritics in the scanned are unreliable; the page scan carry the marks.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone illustrated on citation forms (verb infinitives in -za and nouns); the article's data are one speaker from Ombatse, Oct. 1983.
new_statements.identity_note: The only opened primary description is Goyvaerts 1986, whose data are 'Kaliko' of Ombatse village (3.18N 30.40E, c. 70 km N of Aru, Zaire), one speaker, Oct. 1983. Glottolog assigns this to Omi [omi] ('Ombatse.. probably = Omi'); the Boone & Watson 1999 survey treats Zairean Kaliko as Kaliko-Omi + Kaliko-Ma'di, both in the collectivite d'Omi, and Ombatse lies near the Glottolog Omi centroid (3.25N 30.54E). Sudanese Keliko is a separate Glottolog language, keli1248 [kbo]; Tucker 1940's Keliko section concerns that variety, not Omi.
